bibliography.abstract: Construction industry scholars have advocated increasing digitalization as a harbinger of manifold improvements, from safe training to efficient waste management. Small construction enterprises, which often face greater difficulties in embracing such a paradigm, are frequently overlooked in investigations of stakeholders' views on technical innovation. This study aims to start filling this gap by investigating the views of small construction enterprises on technical innovation. We report the themes that emerged from the qualitative analysis of interviews with construction artisans in North-East Italy in 2018-2019, including installers, restorers, carpenters, painters, and upholsterers (N=25). We asked what makes new technical devices acceptable to them and conducted inductive and deductive thematic analyses to identify recurrent arguments supporting their positions. The analysis identified fifteen premises underlying the interviewees' positions on technical innovation, grouped around four issues: Is technological innovation part of my job? Is the financial cost of innovating worthwhile? Will the new technology be practical? What part of my business is served by communication devices? The study sheds more light on an underrepresented sector and the articulated view of technological innovation in small enterprises, where there is no distance between investors and users. It also adopts a qualitative methodology that can be exported to investigate the acceptability requirements of other samples and specific devices.
bibliography.title: "You should see my partners' fingers": A Qualitative Study of Construction Artisans' Perspective on Technical Innovation

en.caveats: The findings are based on a small qualitative sample of 25 artisans in a single region of Italy, which may limit their generalizability to larger firms or different cultural contexts.
en.what: This study analyzes the perspectives of 25 construction artisans, including installers, restorers, carpenters, painters, and upholsterers, on technical innovation in North-East Italy using interviews conducted in 2018-2019. Through inductive and deductive thematic analysis, the researchers identified fifteen underlying premises regarding technology adoption, categorized into four core themes: professional identity, financial viability, practical usability, and the role of communication devices.
en.why: It provides empirical evidence on how small construction enterprises evaluate technology, revealing that decision-making in these firms is highly integrated because the investor and the end-user are the same person.
